summary:
NASA has watched wildfires from space since 2000, but its two fire-detecting instruments don’t agree. The older MODIS sensors see the Earth in 1 km pixels; the newer VIIRS sensors, active since 2012, use 375 m pixels and report about four times more hotspots for the same fires. If we simply joined the two records, it would look like fires went up four times when VIIRS arrived. And if we translated MODIS up to VIIRS, we would be inventing fires that no satellite ever saw.

We built Harmonic Heat, a website that harmonizes both records into one consistent fire history from 2000 to 2026. Using 591 million NASA FIRMS detections, our pipeline converts VIIRS down into MODIS-equivalent units for every region and month, and tests itself on years it never saw: the 4x gap shrinks to about 1%, with a 0.99 correlation.

This matters because MODIS is retiring: Terra and Aqua are aging and drifting, and soon only VIIRS will remain. VIIRS catches smaller fires, but only MODIS reaches back to 2000, so any 25-year fire trend must be measured in MODIS terms. By learning from the 2012–2026 years when both sensors watched the same fires, Harmonic Heat lets the MODIS record continue on VIIRS without a fake jump. Firefighters, land managers, and scientists can draw any area and see whether a month was truly unusual compared with 25 years of history.
details:
Harmonic Heat combines NASA’s two satellite records of fire detections into a single fire history for 2000–2026.

How it works: The older NASA MODIS sensors view the Earth at 1 km resolution; the newer VIIRS sensors use 375 m resolution and report roughly four times as many hotspots for the same fires. Combined naively, the series shows a false jump in 2012. The pipeline cleans 591 million NASA FIRMS detections, compares both sensors where they overlap, and learns a transformation from VIIRS to MODIS units for each region and season. The algorithm self-tests on unseen years and shrinks the 4x gap to about 1%, with a correlation of 0.99.

Benefit and impact: Any user can select any region or draw an arbitrary area and immediately get a “burning calendar”: when fires occur, whether a month is abnormal, and how seasons compare over 26 years. Results are downloadable as CSV or Excel files, and every view can be shared as a link.

Tools: Python (pandas, DuckDB, NumPy); React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and D3; Cloudflare Pages and R2; NASA FIRMS fire data and NASA GIBS imagery.

Innovation: Rather than fabricate fires that MODIS never detected, we translate VIIRS down into MODIS units, so the long record stays honest. All calculations run in the visitor’s browser, with no server needed.

Factors we considered: data honesty, fast loading on slow connections, and an open, reproducible method.
